Series::sort¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::sort() const -> Series
Series::sort(std::int64_t dim) const -> Series
Series::sort(std::int64_t dim, bool descending) const -> Series
Series::sort(std::int64_t dim, bool descending, bool stable) const -> Series

What It Does¶

sort() returns values in order and leaves the source unchanged. It is a within-axis transformation: it never combines values across unrelated lanes. By default it orders the final axis ascending. dim chooses another axis, descending changes direction, and stable controls the relative order of equal values.

Use sort_pair() when sorted values and their original positions must be returned together.

Parameters¶

dim (std::int64_t): axis to order. Negative dimensions count from the end.

descending (bool): false gives smallest-to-largest; true gives largest-to-smallest.

stable (bool): preserve equal values’ source order when true. With false, their order has no public guarantee.

Returns¶

sort() returns ordered values with the source shape and dtype.

Gradient¶

sort() moves values without altering them, so its value channel is differentiable: in backpropagation each output’s gradient is routed back to the position that value held in the input. What is not differentiable is the ordering itself — which input position maps to which rank is a discrete function of the data, held fixed during the backward pass, so no gradient flows through a rank change when two values cross.

Examples¶

Example 1. The default sorts the final axis ascending.

auto scores = pluss::make_series({3.0, 1.0, 4.0, 1.0, 5.0});
pluss::series::print(std::cout, scores.sort());

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[1.0000, 1.0000, 3.0000, 4.0000, 5.0000]

Example 2. Descending order selects the opposite ordering direction.

std::cout << scores.sort(0, true);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[5, 4, 3, 1, 1]

Example 3. Axis choice changes which values compete. dim=0 orders down each column; dim=-1 orders across each row.

auto table = pluss::make_series({{4.0, 1.0, 3.0}, {2.0, 5.0, 1.0}});
std::cout << table.sort(0) << "\n";
std::cout << table.sort(-1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[1,2], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=false)
data=[[2, 1, 1],
  [4, 5, 3]]
pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[1, 3, 4],
  [1, 2, 5]]

The first result is non-contiguous because the ordered axis is not final. That is a layout detail, not a different value ordering.

Example 4. An absent dimension is rejected rather than interpreted as a flat sort.

try { std::cout << scores.sort(1); }
catch (const std::exception& error) { std::cout << error.what(); }

Output¶

sort: dim out of range

Example 5. The value channel is differentiable — a weighted sum of the sorted values sends each weight back to the position that supplied that rank.

auto x = pluss::make_series({3.0, 1.0, 4.0, 1.0, 5.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto weights = pluss::make_series({10.0, 20.0, 30.0, 40.0, 50.0});
(x.sort() * weights).sum().reverse();

pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[30.0000, 10.0000, 40.0000, 20.0000, 50.0000]

The ascending order is [1, 1, 3, 4, 5], drawn from input positions [1, 3, 0, 2, 4], so weight 30 (the third) lands on position 0, weight 40 on position 2, and so on.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • sort() returns values; argsort() returns the indices needed to recreate the order.

  • Equal-value ordering is a contract only with stable=true.

  • Sorting non-final axes can produce a non-contiguous result. Call contiguous() only when a downstream operation requires contiguous layout.

  • The value channel is differentiable; the ordering decision is not.

  • Complex-valued inputs are rejected.

Summary¶

Use sort() for a complete ordered value sequence and sort_pair() whenever the source positions must travel with that sequence.
